claim: All four FGF receptors are present in the surface ectoderm during lens induction.
source: Previous studies have established the presence of all four FGF receptors in the surface ectoderm during lens induction (Garcia et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Garcia et al., 2011

claim: Deletion of Fgfr1 and Fgfr2 results only in thinning of the lens placode with no discernible impact on lens determination transcription factors like Pax6, Sox2, and Foxe3.
source: However, despite the deletion of the primary FGFRs, Fgfr1, and Fgfr2, only thinning of the lens placode occurred, with no discernible impact on lens determination transcription factors like Pax6, Sox2, and Foxe3.
evidence: Stated as a finding from previous studies

claim: Pax6Le-Cre activity is present within the lens placode at E9.5.
source: The Pax6Le-Cre activity within the lens placode at E9.5, as indicated by the embedded GFP reporter (Figure 1B, arrows), resulted in the complete loss of pERK in the ectoderm, confirming FGF signaling inactivation (Figure 1B, inserts and arrowheads).
evidence: Demonstrated by GFP reporter expression in Figure 1B

claim: Deletion of all four FGFRs results in complete loss of pERK in the ectoderm.
source: The Pax6Le-Cre activity within the lens placode at E9.5, as indicated by the embedded GFP reporter (Figure 1B, arrows), resulted in the complete loss of pERK in the ectoderm, confirming FGF signaling inactivation (Figure 1B, inserts and arrowheads).
evidence: Shown by pERK staining in Figure 1B

claim: In Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1f/f;Fgfr2f/f;Fgfr3f/f;Fgfr4-/- mutants, Pax6 expression persists but Sox2 expression fails to be upregulated.
source: Consequently, while the initial marker of lens induction, increased Pax6 expression as the surface ectoderm transitions into the lens placode, persisted in the mutant, Sox2 expression failed to be upregulated.
evidence: Observed in mutant analysis shown in Figure 1B

claim: Lens placode invagination is driven by apical constriction evidenced by polarized F-actin localization on the apical side by E10.5.
source: Furthermore, subsequent lens placode invagination, driven by apical constriction evidenced by polarized F-actin localization on the apical side by E10.5 (Chauhan et al., 2011), was disrupted (Figure 1C arrows).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chauhan et al., 2011 and shown in Figure 1C

claim: Deletion of all four FGFRs disrupts lens placode invagination.
source: Furthermore, subsequent lens placode invagination, driven by apical constriction evidenced by polarized F-actin localization on the apical side by E10.5 (Chauhan et al., 2011), was disrupted (Figure 1C arrows).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 1C

claim: Overall cell polarity remains unaffected in Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1f/f;Fgfr2f/f;Fgfr3f/f;Fgfr4-/- mutants despite disrupted apical constriction.
source: This occurred despite the proper localization of Fibronectin at the basal side of the lens placode (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that overall cell polarity remained unaffected.
evidence: Inferred from Fibronectin localization shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1f/f;Fgfr2f/f;Fgfr3f/f;Fgfr4-/- mutants fail to exhibit upregulation of Foxe3 and Jag1 in lens vesicle.
source: The Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1f/f;Fgfr2f/f;Fgfr3f/f;Fgfr4-/- mutant also failed to exhibit the expected upregulation of Foxe3 and Jag1 in lens vesicle, further underscoring impaired lens induction (Figure 1C, arrowheads).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1C

claim: The dorsal-to-ventral gradient of BMP signaling persists in Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1f/f;Fgfr2f/f;Fgfr3f/f;Fgfr4-/- knockouts.
source: Previous studies have highlighted FGF and BMP interaction during lens formation (Garcia et al., 2011), yet the dorsal-to-ventral gradient of BMP signaling, as indicated by pSmad staining, persisted in Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1f/f;Fgfr2f/f;Fgfr3f/f;Fgfr4-/- knockouts (Figure 1D, arrowheads).
evidence: Demonstrated by pSmad staining in Figure 1D

claim: Wnt signaling shows no signs of abnormal activity in Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1f/f;Fgfr2f/f;Fgfr3f/f;Fgfr4-/- mutants.
source: Furthermore, Wnt signaling, a known negative regulator of lens induction (Smith et al., 2005), showed no signs of abnormal activity, as indicated by the absence of Lef1 expression (Figure 1D, arrows).
evidence: Shown by Lef1 expression analysis in Figure 1D

claim: FGF signaling is required independently of Bmp and Wnt signaling for lens induction.
source: These results demonstrated that FGF signaling is required independently of Bmp and Wnt signaling for lens induction.
evidence: Concluded from the persistence of BMP and Wnt signaling in FGFR mutants

claim: Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1f/f;Fgfr2f/f mutant lens cells show apical confinement of F-actin and expression of Foxe3.
source: In contrast to mutants with deletion of all four FGFRs, we observed apical confinement of F-actin and expression of Foxe3 in the Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1f/f;Fgfr2f/f mutant lens cells, although the number of Foxe3-expressing cells were reduced (Figure 1E and H, arrows).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1E and H

claim: The number of Foxe3-expressing cells is reduced in Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1f/f;Fgfr2f/f mutants.
source: In contrast to mutants with deletion of all four FGFRs, we observed apical confinement of F-actin and expression of Foxe3 in the Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1f/f;Fgfr2f/f mutant lens cells, although the number of Foxe3-expressing cells were reduced (Figure 1E and H, arrows).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 1H

claim: Deletion of Fgfr1/2 disrupts mTOR signaling in the lens vesicle.
source: However, there was a conspicuous reduction in phosphorylation of mTOR and its downstream target S6 in the lens vesicle, suggesting that deletion of Fgfr1/2 disrupted mTOR signaling (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D, arrowheads).
evidence: Shown by reduced pmTOR and pS6 staining in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D

claim: Prox1 and αA crystallin expression is lost in Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1f/f;Fgfr2f/f mutant lens vesicle.
source: Underscoring the lens differentiation defect, Prox1, a crucial transcription factor for lens fiber development, along with the lens-specific protein αA crystallin expression, was also lost in the Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1f/f;Fgfr2f/f mutant lens vesicle (Figure 1F, arrows) (Garg et al., 2020; Ochi et al., 2003; Xie et al., 2016).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1F and supported by citations

claim: Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1f/f;Fgfr2f/f mutants show decreased Cyclin D1 expression in the lens vesicle.
source: Additionally, there was a notable decrease in Cyclin D1 expression and increasing TUNEL staining within the lens vesicle, indicating cell proliferation and apoptosis defects (Figure 1G, I and J, arrows and arrowheads) (Garcia et al., 2011).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1G and quantified in Figure 1I

claim: Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1f/f;Fgfr2f/f mutants show increased TUNEL staining in the lens vesicle.
source: Additionally, there was a notable decrease in Cyclin D1 expression and increasing TUNEL staining within the lens vesicle, indicating cell proliferation and apoptosis defects (Figure 1G, I and J, arrows and arrowheads) (Garcia et al., 2011).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1G and quantified in Figure 1J

claim: The constitutively active KrasG12D allele effectively restores pERK expression in Fgfr1/2 mutants.
source: When crossed with Fgfr1/2 mutants, this allele effectively restored pERK expression and normalized lens vesicle invagination (Figure 2B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2B

claim: The constitutively active KrasG12D allele normalizes lens vesicle invagination in Fgfr1/2 mutants.
source: When crossed with Fgfr1/2 mutants, this allele effectively restored pERK expression and normalized lens vesicle invagination (Figure 2B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2B

claim: Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1f/f;Fgfr2f/f;KrasG12D lens displays robust phosphorylation of MEK at E13.5.
source: By E13.5, the Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1f/f;Fgfr2f/f;KrasG12D lens displayed robust phosphorylation of MEK, the upstream kinase of Erk, concomitant with the expression of lens fiber markers Prox1 and αA crystallin (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2B and C

claim: Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1f/f;Fgfr2f/f;KrasG12D lens expresses lens fiber markers Prox1 and αA crystallin at E13.5.
source: By E13.5, the Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1f/f;Fgfr2f/f;KrasG12D lens displayed robust phosphorylation of MEK, the upstream kinase of Erk, concomitant with the expression of lens fiber markers Prox1 and αA crystallin (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2B and C

claim: The rescued Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1f/f;Fgfr2f/f;KrasG12D lens reaches about half the size of a control lens.
source: Notably, the rescued lens reached about half the size of a control lens (Figure 2D).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 2D

claim: Kras signaling acts as a primary conduit for FGF signaling during lens development.
source: These results suggest that Kras signaling acts as a primary conduit for FGF signaling during lens development.
evidence: Concluded from the rescue experiments with KrasG12D

claim: Deletion of Bax and Bak in Fgfr1/2 mutants suppresses apoptosis.
source: To ascertain whether cell death underpins the pronounced lens vesicle defect in Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1f/f;Fgfr2f/f mutant, we targeted Bax and Bak, two core regulators of the intrinsic pathway of apoptosis, for deletion. This intervention notably reduced TUNEL signals within the lens placode (Figure 2E and F)
evidence: Shown in Figure 2E and quantified in Figure 2G

claim: Deletion of Bax and Bak in Fgfr1/2 mutants results in recovery of lens formation.
source: and resulted in a recovery of lens formation, as evidenced by the expression of Foxe3, Maf, and Jag1 (Figure 2G), although the lens remained considerably smaller than the wild-type control (Figure 2H).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2F and quantified in Figure 2H

claim: FGF signaling plays a critical role in preventing excessive cell apoptosis during lens development.
source: This underscores the critical role of FGF signaling in preventing excessive cell apoptosis during lens development.
evidence: Concluded from the Bax/Bak deletion rescue experiments

claim: The Frs2 binding site has been mapped to the juxtamembrane domain of FGFR.
source: Previous studies have mapped the Frs2 binding site to the juxtamembrane domain of FGFR (Dhalluin et al., 2000; Ong et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dhalluin et al., 2000 and Ong et al., 2000

claim: The Fgfr1/2 compound mutant carrying Fgfr1ΔFrs mirrors the null phenotype.
source: Intriguingly, while the Fgfr1/2 compound mutant carrying Fgfr1ΔFrs mirrored the null phenotype (Figure 3B, arrowheads), the mutant featuring Fgfr2LR exhibited sustained expression of pERK, Cyclin D1, and αA crystallin, with no discernible increase in cell death, as confirmed by cleaved caspase 3 staining (see Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3B

claim: The mutant featuring Fgfr2LR exhibits sustained expression of pERK, Cyclin D1, and αA crystallin.
source: Intriguingly, while the Fgfr1/2 compound mutant carrying Fgfr1ΔFrs mirrored the null phenotype (Figure 3B, arrowheads), the mutant featuring Fgfr2LR exhibited sustained expression of pERK, Cyclin D1, and αA crystallin, with no discernible increase in cell death, as confirmed by cleaved caspase 3 staining (see Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3B and C

claim: The juxtamembrane domain of FGFR likely serves additional functions beyond Frs2 binding in lens induction.
source: This suggests that the juxtamembrane domain of FGFR likely serves additional functions beyond Frs2 binding in lens induction.
evidence: Inferred from the different phenotypes of Fgfr1ΔFrs and Fgfr2LR mutants

claim: Fgfr3 expression in the murine lens rapidly increases from E11.5 onwards.
source: Upon examining the iSyTE lens gene expression database (Kakrana et al., 2018), we observed a rapid increase in Fgfr3 expression in the murine lens from E11.5 onwards, surpassing the levels of both Fgfr1 and Fgfr2 by E12.5 (Figure 3D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3D from iSyTE database

claim: Fgfr3 expression surpasses the levels of both Fgfr1 and Fgfr2 by E12.5 in the murine lens.
source: Upon examining the iSyTE lens gene expression database (Kakrana et al., 2018), we observed a rapid increase in Fgfr3 expression in the murine lens from E11.5 onwards, surpassing the levels of both Fgfr1 and Fgfr2 by E12.5 (Figure 3D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3D

claim: Deletion of Fgfr3 in conjunction with Fgfr1 and Fgfr2LR impedes the differentiation and elongation of posterior lens epithelial cells.
source: To explore this hypothesis, we further deleted Fgfr3 in conjunction with the Fgfr1 and Fgfr2LR mutant, which indeed impeded the differentiation and elongation of posterior lens epithelial cells, as evidenced by the absence of αA crystallin, Jag1, and Maf at E11.5 (Figure 3E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3E

claim: Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1f/f;Fgfr2f/LR;Fgfr3f/f triple mutant remains a hollow lens vesicle without any pERK expression at E12.5.
source: By E12.5, unlike the Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1f/f;Fgfr2f/LR mutant, which retained pERK staining and generated lens fibers to populate the lens vesicle similar to controls, the Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1f/f;Fgfr2f/LR;Fgfr3f/f triple mutant remained a hollow lens vesicle without any pERK expression (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3F and G

claim: The Frs2 binding site on FGFR is dispensable for lens induction and lens vesicle formation.
source: Thus, while the Frs2 binding site on FGFR is dispensable for lens induction and lens vesicle formation, it evidently emerges as crucial for the later stage of lens fiber differentiation.
evidence: Concluded from the analysis of Fgfr2LR mutants

claim: The Frs2 binding site on FGFR is crucial for lens fiber differentiation.
source: Thus, while the Frs2 binding site on FGFR is dispensable for lens induction and lens vesicle formation, it evidently emerges as crucial for the later stage of lens fiber differentiation.
evidence: Concluded from the analysis of Fgfr2LR mutants combined with Fgfr3 deletion

claim: Pax6Le-Cre;Grb2f/f mutant forms a lens vesicle at E12.5 but lacks pERK staining.
source: Indeed, the Pax6Le-Cre;Grb2f/f mutant formed a lens vesicle at E12.5 but lacked pERK staining, correlating with decreased Cyclin D3 expression and increased TUNEL staining (Figure 4A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4A

claim: Pax6Le-Cre;Grb2f/f mutant shows decreased Cyclin D3 expression at E12.5.
source: Indeed, the Pax6Le-Cre;Grb2f/f mutant formed a lens vesicle at E12.5 but lacked pERK staining, correlating with decreased Cyclin D3 expression and increased TUNEL staining (Figure 4A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4A

claim: Pax6Le-Cre;Grb2f/f mutant shows increased TUNEL staining at E12.5.
source: Indeed, the Pax6Le-Cre;Grb2f/f mutant formed a lens vesicle at E12.5 but lacked pERK staining, correlating with decreased Cyclin D3 expression and increased TUNEL staining (Figure 4A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4A

claim: In Pax6Le-Cre;Grb2f/f mutants, Foxe3 is unaffected but Jag1 is absent and Maf and crystallin are reduced.
source: Notably, the initial lens determination gene Foxe3 was unaffected, but differentiation marker Jag1 was absent while Maf and crystallin were reduced.
evidence: Observed in Figure 4A

claim: Deletion of Grb2 results in significant reduction in expression of Cyclin D1, p57, and Prox1 at E11.5.
source: This lens differentiation defect is evident as early as E11.5, characterized by a significant reduction in the expression of cell cycle regulators Cyclin D1 and p57, as well as the pro-differentiation transcription factor Prox1, suggesting dysregulation of the cell cycle and failure to initiate the lens fiber cell differentiation program (Figure 4B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4B

claim: By E13.5, the Pax6Le-Cre;Grb2f/f lens vesicle remains hollow and smaller compared to the control.
source: By E13.5, the lens vesicle remained hollow and smaller compared to the control (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4B and quantified in Figure 4C

claim: Grb2 is the primary downstream effector of Frs2 in promoting lens fiber differentiation.
source: The deletion of Grb2 affects lens differentiation without hindering the formation of the lens vesicle, mirroring the effect of Frs2 binding site mutation, thus supporting the notion that Grb2 is the primary downstream effector of Frs2 in promoting lens fiber differentiation.
evidence: Concluded from comparison of Grb2 and Frs2 binding site mutation phenotypes

claim: Mutations in the Shp2 binding sites on Frs2 led to severe eye development defects.
source: While both Frs2 and Shp2 possess phosphotyrosine residues that can engage with Grb2 (Figure 5A), it's noteworthy that only mutations in the Shp2 binding sites, rather than those in the Grb2 binding sites on Frs2, led to severe eye development defects (Gotoh et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gotoh et al., 2004

claim: Homozygous mice carrying the Shp2YF mutation die around E12.5.
source: However, homozygous mice carrying the Shp2YF mutation died around E12.5 with visibly paler and smaller bodies (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5D and E

claim: Shp2YF/YF mutants have a significantly thinner labyrinth zone in placentas.
source: Histological analysis of mutants revealed a significantly thinner labyrinth zone in placentas, crucial for oxygen and nutrient supplies (Figure 5E, dotted lines).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5E

claim: Sox2Cre;Shp2f/YF embryos survive past embryonic day 15.5 without evident morphological abnormalities.
source: Sox2Cre;Shp2f/YF embryos indeed survived past embryonic day 15.5 without evident morphological abnormalities, yet they succumbed shortly after birth for reasons yet unknown (Figure 5G).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5G

claim: Phosphorylation of Shp2 (pShp2Y542) induced by FGF is abolished in Sox2Cre;Shp2f/YF MEF cells.
source: As anticipated, the phosphorylation of Shp2 (pShp2Y542) induced by FGF was abolished in Sox2Cre;Shp2f/YF MEF cells, yet the activation of pERK was only partially impaired (Figure 5H).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5H

claim: The activation of pERK is only partially impaired in Sox2Cre;Shp2f/YF MEF cells upon FGF stimulation.
source: As anticipated, the phosphorylation of Shp2 (pShp2Y542) induced by FGF was abolished in Sox2Cre;Shp2f/YF MEF cells, yet the activation of pERK was only partially impaired (Figure 5H).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5H

claim: Sox2Cre;Shp2f/YF MEF cells show a more pronounced reduction in pERK response to PDGF stimulation compared to FGF stimulation.
source: This contrasts with the more pronounced reduction in PDGF-induced ERK phosphorylation, underscoring a distinct requirement for Shp2-Grb2 binding across related receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) pathways (Araki et al., 2003).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5H and supported by citation to Araki et al., 2003

claim: Neither the pattern of pERK staining nor the size of the lens shows discernible alterations in Sox2Cre;Shp2f/YF mutants.
source: In line with the subtle impact on FGF signaling, neither the pattern of pERK staining nor the size of the lens showed discernible alterations in Sox2Cre;Shp2f/YF mutants (Figure 5I, arrowheads).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5I

claim: Sox2Cre;Shp2f/YF mutants show a slight reduction in pERK staining in the lacrimal gland primordia at E14.5.
source: Notably, we observed a slight reduction in pERK staining in the lacrimal gland primordia at E14.5 and fewer lacrimal gland buds at birth (Figure 5I, arrows).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5I

claim: Sox2Cre;Shp2f/YF mutants have fewer lacrimal gland buds at birth.
source: Notably, we observed a slight reduction in pERK staining in the lacrimal gland primordia at E14.5 and fewer lacrimal gland buds at birth (Figure 5I, arrows).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5I and quantified in Figure 5J

claim: Shp2-Grb2 binding exerts a modest influence on FGF signaling.
source: These nuanced ocular phenotypes, alongside the overall normal morphology of Sox2Cre;Shp2f/YF mutant embryos, collectively suggest that Shp2-Grb2 binding exerts a modest influence on FGF signaling.
evidence: Concluded from the mild phenotypes observed in Sox2Cre;Shp2f/YF mutants

claim: Y209 is the most frequently phosphorylated tyrosine residue in Grb2 according to the PhosphoSitePlus database.
source: Based on the PhosphoSitePlus database, we identified Y209 as the most frequently phosphorylated tyrosine residue in Grb2 (Figure 6A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6A from PhosphoSitePlus database

claim: Shp2 dephosphorylates Y209 on Grb2 upon stimulation by various receptor tyrosine kinases.
source: Notably, previous studies have demonstrated that Shp2 dephosphorylates this specific site upon stimulation by various receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) (Ahmed et al., 2013; Haines et al., 2009; Li et al., 2001; Riera et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ahmed et al., 2013; Haines et al., 2009; Li et al., 2001; Riera et al., 2010

claim: Grb2YF/YF homozygous mutants exhibit normal viability and fertility without any obvious phenotype.
source: Surprisingly, our findings revealed that Grb2YF/YF homozygous mutants exhibited normal viability and fertility without any obvious phenotype.
evidence: Observed in the generated Grb2YF mutant mice

claim: The intensity of pERK staining in Grb2YF/YF mutant lenses remains unchanged compared to controls.
source: Additionally, the intensity of pERK staining in mutant lenses remained unchanged in mutant lenses compared to controls, and markers of the cell cycle (Ki67 and p57) as well as differentiation (Jag1, Foxe3, and Maf) were unaffected (Figure 6D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6D

claim: Y209 on Grb2 is dispensable for FGF signaling.
source: These results suggest that despite being a frequent target for phosphorylation, Y209 on Grb2 is dispensable for FGF signaling.
evidence: Concluded from the lack of phenotype in Grb2YF mutants

claim: Shp2CS/CS embryos exhibit stunted growth but survive until E9.5.
source: Unlike the earlier Shp2 null mutants that perished by E7.5 (Yang et al., 2006), Shp2CS/CS embryos exhibited stunted growth but survived until E9.5, indicating that the Shp2CS mutation doesn't entirely abrogate Shp2's function (Figure 6G).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6G and compared to Yang et al., 2006

claim: Shp2f/CS MEF cells retain considerable pERK activity in response to FGF stimulation after Cre-mediated deletion.
source: Moreover, after removing the flox allele using Cre-expressing adenovirus, the Shp2f/CS MEF cells still retained considerable pERK activity in response to FGF stimulation (Figure 6H).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6H

claim: pERK is detected in Pax6Le-Cre;Shp2f/CS lens but not in Pax6Le-Cre;Shp2f/f mutants.
source: This was mirrored in vivo, with pERK detection in the Pax6Le-Cre;Shp2f/CS lens but not in the Pax6Le-Cre;Shp2f/f mutants (Figure 6I).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6I

claim: Lens epithelial cells in Pax6Le-Cre;Shp2f/f mutants migrate to the posterior pole with reduced p57 and Jag1 expression.
source: Consequently, lens epithelial cells in Pax6Le-Cre;Shp2f/f mutants migrated to the posterior pole with reduced p57 and Jag1 expression, indicating impaired differentiation, but Pax6Le-Cre;Shp2f/CS lens epithelial cells showed proper p57-mediated cell cycle exit at the lens equator and initiated timely expression of Jag1 (Figure 6J).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6I

claim: Pax6Le-Cre;Shp2f/CS lens epithelial cells show proper p57-mediated cell cycle exit at the lens equator and timely expression of Jag1.
source: Consequently, lens epithelial cells in Pax6Le-Cre;Shp2f/f mutants migrated to the posterior pole with reduced p57 and Jag1 expression, indicating impaired differentiation, but Pax6Le-Cre;Shp2f/CS lens epithelial cells showed proper p57-mediated cell cycle exit at the lens equator and initiated timely expression of Jag1 (Figure 6J).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6I

claim: Pax6Le-Cre;Shp2f/CS lenses show normal proliferation (Ki67) but increased cell death (TUNEL).
source: However, these lenses showed normal proliferation (Ki67) but increased cell death (TUNEL), resulting in a smaller size (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Development of the lacrimal gland is blocked in both Pax6Le-Cre;Shp2f/f and Pax6Le-Cre;Shp2f/CS mutants.
source: Moreover, the development of the FGF signaling-sensitive lacrimal gland was blocked in both Pax6Le-Cre;Shp2f/f and Pax6Le-Cre;Shp2f/CS mutants, a more pronounced effect than the modest reduction in lacrimal gland buds observed in Shp2YF/YF mutants (Figure 6I).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6I

claim: Inhibiting Shp2's phosphatase activity more significantly affects FGF signaling compared to obstructing its adaptor function.
source: This suggests that inhibiting Shp2's phosphatase activity more significantly affects FGF signaling compared to obstructing its adaptor function, yet doesn't completely abolish FGF signaling.
evidence: Concluded from comparison of Shp2CS and Shp2YF phenotypes

claim: FGF stimulation is ineffective in raising pFrs2 and pShp2 levels in both Fgfr1f/ΔFrs;Fgfr2f/f and Fgfr1f/f;Fgfr2f/LR MEF cells after Cre-mediated deletion.
source: Interestingly, FGF stimulation was ineffective in raising pFrs2 and pShp2 levels in both sets of MEF cells and did not alter the phosphorylation states of Crk and Gab1, both recognized adaptors in FGF signaling (Collins et al., 2018; Hadari et al., 2001; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7A and supported by citations

claim: Shc phosphorylation is lost in Fgfr1f/ΔFrs;Fgfr2f/f cells but persists in Fgfr1f/f;Fgfr2f/LR mutants upon FGF stimulation.
source: However, a key difference emerged – Shc phosphorylation was lost in Fgfr1f/ΔFrs;Fgfr2f/f cells but persisted in Fgfr1f/f;Fgfr2f/LR mutants (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7A and quantified in Figure 7B

claim: pShc is detectable in both wild-type and Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1f/f;Fgfr2f/LR lens vesicles, but not in Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1f/ΔFrs;Fgfr2f/f mutants.
source: This observation was further supported by in vivo data, which showed that pShc was detectable in both wild-type and Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1f/f;Fgfr2f/LR lens vesicles, but not in Pax6Le-Cre;Fgfr1f/ΔFrs;Fgfr2f/f mutants (Figure 7C, arrowhead).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7C

claim: Shc can be activated by the FGFR independently of its Frs2 binding site.
source: These findings suggest that Shc can be activated by the FGFR independently of its Frs2 binding site, potentially serving as an alternate route for Grb2's engagement.
evidence: Concluded from the differential Shc phosphorylation in Fgfr mutants

claim: Shc1 is the most abundant Shc gene in the lens among the four Shc genes present in the mammalian genome.
source: Among the four Shc genes present in the mammalian genome, Shc1 is the most abundant in the lens (iSyTE lens gene expression database).
evidence: Based on iSyTE lens gene expression database

claim: Pax6Le-Cre;Shc1f/f lenses display only minor reductions in pERK staining and size.
source: However, Pax6Le-Cre;Shc1f/f lenses displayed only minor reductions in pERK staining and size, suggesting potential redundancy with other Shc proteins or compensatory mechanisms involving Frs2 and Shp2 (Figure 7D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7D

claim: Deletion of Frs2 or Shp2 alone leads to a modest diminution in lens size.
source: We have previously reported that the deletion of Frs2 or Shp2 alone led to a modest diminution in lens size, akin to the Shc1 deletion effect.
evidence: Reported in previous publication by the authors

claim: The combined knockout of Frs2 and Shp2 results in hollow lens vesicles.
source: However, the combined knockout of Frs2 and Shp2 (Pax6Le-Cre;Frs2f/f;Shp2f/f) resulted in hollow lens vesicles, highlighting a synergistic interaction between these two genes (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: Reported in Li et al., 2014

claim: Introducing the Shc1 knockout into the Pax6Le-Cre;Frs2f/f;Shp2f/f background further diminishes the lens size.
source: While the Pax6Le-Cre;Frs2f/f;Shc1f/f compound mutant did not exhibit as severe abnormalities, introducing the Shc1 knockout into the Pax6Le-Cre;Frs2f/f;Shp2f/f background further diminished the lens size, suggesting that Shc1 contributes an additive role alongside Frs2 and Shp2 in modulating lens development (Figure 7E–F).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7E and quantified in Figure 7F

claim: Shc1 functions independently of Frs2 and Shp2 to transmit FGF signaling in lens development.
source: These findings collectively showed that Shc1 functions independently of Frs2 and Shp2 to transmit FGF signaling in lens development.
evidence: Concluded from the compound mutant analysis

claim: The lens placode emerges as thickened epithelia within the lateral head ectoderm at E9.5 in mice.
source: In mice, the lens placode emerges as thickened epithelia within the lateral head ectoderm at E9.5 (Figure 1A).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge and shown in Figure 1A

claim: The lens placode undergoes invagination to form the lens pit at E10.5.
source: It undergoes invagination to form the lens pit at E10.5, and upon separation from the surface ectoderm, progresses into the lens vesicle at E11.5.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge
